extraction.citation: Hájek M, Petružela L (2016). Sustainability of the public water supply and sewerage services operating system: a case study on the example of the Czech Republic. Scientia Agriculturae Bohemica 47(1):32-39.
extraction.service_provider: municipalities own the infrastructure; public-interest operators, often privately owned and profit-based, run it under exclusive rights for a limited period in a defined area
extraction.regulatory_model: state economic regulation of water and sewerage prices (cost-based pricing under the water law; local monopoly), within EU rules on services of general interest; partial privatisation of operators since the 1990s
extraction.population: Czech households (about 94% supplied from public water systems), by income decile
extraction.sample_size: National statistical series: tariff price and domestic consumption 1994-2012 (Table 1, 19 years) and household water-and-sewerage bills as a share of net income by income decile 2005-2012 (Table 2, 10 deciles x 8 years) from the Czech Statistical Office Household Budget Survey and Income and Living Conditions data, plus Ministry of Agriculture price data; the household survey sample sizes are not stated
extraction.effect_measure: descriptive time-series statistics: Pearson correlation between price and domestic consumption (1994-2012), income elasticity of demand by income decile, water and sewerage bills as a share of net household income (Table 2)
extraction.effect_estimate: Price rose from CZK 9.39 per m3 (1994) to CZK 37.28 (2012) while domestic consumption fell from 696 to 481 million m3; the Pearson correlation is r = 0.91965 (the paper describes a dependence of the decline in consumption on price; the variables' signs are not shown). Water and sewerage bills as a share of net household income (Table 2): decile 1 2.52-2.74% across 2005-2012, decile 10 0.73-0.91%, deciles 2-9 between 1.07% and 2.06%. Taking expenditure above 2% (2-3%) of net income as water poverty, the authors say it occurs covertly in about a third of households and rises to as much as 25% in years of economic decline, and that households in decile 4 and below diverge from decile 5 and above; income elasticity of demand is mostly inelastic (below 1) and higher in the first of two four-year periods. The text and Table 2 disagree: the text says decile 4 moved into water poverty from 2009, but Table 2 gives decile 4 at 1.52-1.88%, below the 2% line. The authors tie declining consumption to the government's method of price regulation and suggest block-rate (social) tariffs.
extraction.extraction_sample_size: national series, 1994-2012 (price and consumption); 10 income deciles x 8 years (bills)
extraction.model_type: descriptive analysis of national time series with correlation and elasticity calculations
extraction.study_design: descriptive secondary-data analysis of national time series (observational; no comparator)
extraction.risk_of_bias_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies
extraction.risk_of_bias_rating: High concern (appraised 2026-10-13 on the full text against the JBI Cross Sectional checklist; items 1-8: Unclear (no sample definition; national statistics), Yes (Czech Republic, data sources named), Yes (tariff prices from official series), Yes (water-poverty threshold of 2-3% of net income), No (confounders not identified), No (no strategy for confounders), Unclear (bills from the Household Budget Survey; the paper notes a discrepancy between recalculated and reported volumes), No (a Pearson correlation on a trended series; elasticity formulas garbled in the text read; text and Table 2 disagree on decile 4); 3/8 Yes)
extraction.selection_bias: Not applicable (national statistical series); household survey sample sizes not stated
extraction.measurement_bias: Moderate (official statistics; text and Table 2 disagree on decile 4; discrepancy between recalculated and reported consumption)
extraction.confounding: High (price and consumption both trend over time; no control for income, housing or technology)
extraction.reporting_bias: Moderate (no pre-specified analysis; some statements are not supported by the tables)
extraction.legal_measurement_quality: low (the regulatory method is described as the context; the regulatory instrument is not measured or compared)
extraction.outcome_measurement_quality: moderate (official household budget statistics; affordability thresholds from the literature)
extraction.section: Full text (journal article, 8 pages): Introduction; Material and methods; Results and discussion (behaviour of consumers, income elasticity of demand, affordability); Conclusion
extraction.exact_location: Table 1 (price and consumption, p. 36); Table 2 (bills as a share of net income by decile, p. 37); Conclusion (p. 37-38)
extraction.extraction_note: New inclusion by the PI's A16 adjudication of 2026-10-13 (narrow reading of criterion 2: state tariff regulation and cost recovery), extracted from the full-text PDF in the researcher's Drive (8 pages read in full as text; the equation rendering is garbled). No effect_sizes.csv row: a descriptive time series with no comparator, standard error or confounder control, and the price-consumption correlation is not an institutional access effect.

evidence_map.evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a descriptive analysis of Czech national statistics (tariff price and domestic consumption 1994-2012; household water-and-sewerage bills as a share of net income by income decile 2005-2012) of how regulated tariff increases relate to consumption and affordability; no comparator or confounder control; read in full text 2026-10-13.
evidence_map.institutional_context: municipal infrastructure owners and (often private) operators under state cost-based tariff regulation (water law) and EU rules on services of general interest
